item.title: SCMBANKER Mexican banking fraud, Accenture breach, and GitHub secret scanning gaps
item.content:encoded:
Accenture confirms breach after hacker offers stolen data for sale — Must Read

Accenture confirmed an isolated security breach after a hacker known as “888” claimed to be selling 35 GB of allegedly stolen source code, keys, tokens, and configuration files. Accenture says it remediated the issue and that operations and service delivery were not impacted, but it has not disclosed what data was accessed or how the breach occurred.

  • Accenture confirmed it suffered an isolated security breach and said it remediated the source of the issue.
  • A threat actor known as "888" claimed to have stolen 35 GB of Accenture data in July 2026 and offered it for sale on a cybercrime forum.
  • The threat actor claimed the stolen data includes source code, RSA keys, SSH keys, Azure personal access tokens, Azure Storage access keys, and configuration files.
  • BleepingComputer said it could not independently verify the full scope of the data that was stolen.
  • Accenture did not disclose how attackers gained access or whether customer data was affected.

ClickFix to Cash-Out: Anatomy of a Mexican Banking-Fraud Toolkit — Should Read

Elastic researchers detailed REF6045, a Mexico-focused banking fraud operation that uses fake CAPTCHA “ClickFix” lures to install the SCMBANKER PowerShell toolkit and let human operators monitor victims, redirect banking sessions, hijack clipboard transfers, run vishing overlays, and deploy Remote Utilities for full access. The case shows how crude, likely AI-assisted malware can still enable effective operator-driven financial theft when paired with social engineering.

  • Elastic Security Labs tracked a Mexican banking fraud operation called REF6045 that uses fake CAPTCHA ClickFix pages to trick victims into running a command that installs the SCMBANKER PowerShell toolkit.
  • SCMBANKER lets operators monitor banking sessions, capture screenshots, display fake bank warning overlays for vishing, redirect browsers to phishing pages, manipulate copied CLABE and card numbers, and deploy Remote Utilities Host for remote access.
  • The toolkit heavily targets Mexico’s financial ecosystem, including retail banks, business banking portals, fintechs, payment processors, cryptocurrency exchanges, investment platforms, SAT, and telecom services.
  • Elastic recovered the operation’s tooling through OPSEC failures including open directories, an exposed web-root archive, and an unauthenticated file editor for live targeting configuration files.
  • The scripts contain strong signs of AI assistance, including document-like comment scaffolding, explanatory comments beside obfuscated code, and inconsistent coding style.

GitHub Secret Scanning Public Monitoring for Enterprises: Coverage and Gaps — Should Read

GitHub’s new public monitoring for enterprise secret scanning helps detect leaked organization secrets across public github.com surfaces, but it only catches exposure after secrets are already public and misses many exfiltration paths such as attacker-controlled endpoints and workflow logs. Enterprises should enable it, but pair it with CI/CD runtime egress controls and broader pipeline leak detection to prevent secrets from leaving in the first place.

  • GitHub’s public monitoring for secret scanning is in public preview for enterprises and scans public content on github.com in real time for an organization’s secrets beyond repositories the enterprise owns.
  • The feature covers public git content, pull request comments, and GitHub issues, and attributes leaks back to an enterprise using GitHub’s identity layer and verified domains.
  • The article says public monitoring does not scan private repositories and cannot see secrets stolen from developer machines or CI environments and sent to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
  • The article notes that workflow run logs are not listed among GitHub’s documented scanned surfaces, even though the tj-actions/changed-files compromise exposed CI/CD credentials in build logs.
  • The article recommends enabling public monitoring for eligible GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers and pairing it with runtime egress control and pipeline leak detection to reduce secret exfiltration risk.
